That flood is what makes git log main..feature terminate at the merge base instead of walking to the dawn of time.

Parsing each commit is parse_commit_buffer, L516: validate the tree line, collect every parent line, and attach them — with graft and shallow-clone substitutions applied where configured. The two orderings git offers fall out cleanly: date order needs nothing extra, while topological order is a post-pass, sort_in_topological_order, L938. The big optimization is the commit-graph file: parse_commit_in_graph, L1075 supplies parent lists and generation numbers straight from a binary index, without inflating or parsing a single commit object — which is exactly why large histories, like the Rust and TypeScript monorepos, stay fast to walk once the graph file is written.

From Clone to First Commit

Building git from source is pleasantly old-school, and the tree verifies it. The canonical instructions in INSTALL are simply make followed by make install — the top-level Makefile drives everything, with build knobs overridable via a config.mak. If you prefer autoconf, make configure regenerates the ./configure script from configure.ac, then ./configure --prefix=/usr && make all doc produces binaries and man pages. There is also a second build system: meson.build is present and documented in build-systems.adoc, and a profile-feedback build (make profile) exists that rebuilds git after running the test suite as training data — the INSTALL notes it buys a few percent on CPU-bound work at the cost of building twice.

You can run the freshly built git without installing: the build tree ships bin-wrappers/, and INSTALL documents prepending it to PATH. First commit is then git commit through the very code path traced above. Notably, the tree now also contains contrib/libgit-rs — early Rust bindings — showing the project slowly exposing its object database beyond C.

Honest Limits

The object model is stable but the hash beneath it is not final. The migration plan from SHA-1 lives in hash-function-transition.adoc: since v2.13.0 git ships a hardened SHA-1 (collision detection, vendored under sha1collisiondetection/), but SHA-1 remains the default algorithm, and the transition is implemented as plumbing — the compat-algo hashing visible in odb_write_object_ext, L696 — rather than a done deal. Repositories like Go that moved hosting around have felt similar storage-format transitions; git’s is still in progress.

Delta compression is also heuristic, not optimal: the window/depth bounds in try_delta, L2802 trade pack size for CPU, and the design doc admits the search is approximate. The index’s stat-based freshness means it can mark clean files dirty after timestamp churn (the racy-git problem, described in racy-git.adoc). And the ref layer is in mid-migration too: files, packed-refs, and reftable backends all coexist, selected per-repository. Finally, the commit-graph is strictly an accelerator — parse_commit_in_graph, L1075 only applies when the file exists and covers your commits; without it, walks inflate every commit object the old way.
entry.summary: How git really stores your history: content-addressed objects, the index, refs and reflogs, packfile delta compression, and commit graph walks — with line-level links into git's C source.

entry.title: Inside Helix: The Selection-First Editor Architecture Explained

link.title: Inside Helix: The Selection-First Editor Architecture Explained

entry.content:
If you have ever spent a weekend assembling a modal editor out of parts — a plugin manager, an LSP config, a tree-sitter setup, a colorscheme written in a DSL — you know the failure mode. The editor itself is fine; the project of making it usable is the problem. Vim and Neovim both solve editing brilliantly, but they ship as kernels: language servers, syntax trees, file pickers, fuzzy finders, all bolted on by configuration or plugins.

Helix, written in Rust, is the opposite bet. It ships the batteries: tree-sitter parsing for every bundled language, an LSP client, a fuzzy picker, theme support, all compiled into a single hx binary with zero plugin ecosystem required. You launch it and a modern editing stack is simply there.

The interesting question is architectural: what actually happens between pressing a key and the buffer changing? We cloned the repository at master (commit 57d864129eb5, workspace version 25.7.1) and traced the whole path. Helix is a Cargo workspace — helix-core (text primitives), helix-view (editor state), helix-term (the application), helix-lsp (language servers), plus smaller crates like helix-event and helix-loader. The diagram below is the map; the rest of this post walks it left to right.

Overview: four crates and one loop. Key presses enter helix-term, become commands, build Transactions in helix-core, land in Documents owned by helix-view, and echo out through the helix-lsp client pool.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A Transaction is not just a text diff — it bundles a ChangeSet with the Selection that should exist after the edit, Transaction, L574. Undo therefore restores your cursors too, not just your text.
  • The ChangeSet is a list of Retain/Delete/Insert operations over the whole buffer, ChangeSet, L73. That invariant makes two change sets composable, which is what lets history, syntax, and LSP all consume the same delta.
  • A Selection is a SmallVec<[Range; 1]> of non-overlapping ranges plus a primary_index, Selection, L417. Multi-cursor is not an add-on; it is the default state of the editor.
  • Each Range stores an anchor and a head, Range, L55. Motions move the head; the anchor is why Kakoune-style “select, then act” works without visual-mode state machines.
  • Document::apply is the single funnel where a transaction hits the buffer, updating history, syntax, and change tracking in one place, Document::apply, L1671.
  • The application loop is a tokio::select! over six event sources — signals, terminal input, job callbacks, status messages, background futures, and editor events, event_loop_until_idle, L307. There is no UI thread in the classic sense; there is one async loop and a redraw request channel.
  • Keystrokes resolve through the default keymap into a MappableCommand, MappableCommand, L214. Every key binding, macro, and typable command funnels through this one enum’s execute.
  • Language servers live behind a Registry that owns a SlotMap<LanguageServerId, Arc<Client>> and merges every server’s incoming calls into one stream, Registry, L581. The loop never talks to a raw LSP process; it talks to that merged stream.

Now zoom into the detail graph, which adds the internal stages: how operations merge, how syntax updates incrementally, and how a server request round-trips.

Detail view: the core editing chain (operations to changesets to transactions), the tree-house syntax stack, the six-branch select! loop, and the LSP registry's client lifecycle.

Ropes, Transactions, and the Selection Model

Helix never edits strings. Buffers are ropey ropes — the workspace pins ropey = "1.6.1" with the simd feature in the root Cargo.toml — because a rope makes an insertion at byte 2,000,000 a cheap local splice instead of a full-copy. On top of ropes sits the change machinery in helix-core/src/transaction.rs.

The Operation enum has exactly three variants — Retain(usize), Delete(usize), and Insert(Tendril), Operation, L13. A ChangeSet is a run-length list of these ops covering the entire buffer; adjacent same-kind ops are merged as they are pushed, and the ops must re-sum to the original rope length. That discipline is what enables ChangeSet::invert, which rebuilds the opposite change set for undo, invert, L609.

Applying is one walk: ChangeSet::apply iterates the rope once, retaining, deleting, and splicing per op, and returns false if the base text does not match what the change set was built against, apply, L342. Transaction::apply wraps that and short-circuits empty change sets, Transaction::apply, L599. The subtle part is the second field: every Transaction carries an optional Selection, so a command like “insert a newline” also states where your cursors end up.

The selection model in helix-core/src/selection.rs is deliberately tiny. A Selection is a SmallVec<[Range; 1]> — one range is inline, no heap allocation for single-cursor editing — plus the index of the primary range, which Selection::primary returns, primary, L428. Adding a range with push makes the new range primary and re-normalizes overlaps. Normalization is what keeps the invariant documented above the struct: a selection can never be empty and ranges never overlap, so consumers never write defensive branches. Motions live in helix-core/src/movement.rs as functions over these ranges, which is why the same motion code serves one cursor or two hundred. On the way into the editor, Document::set_selection stores one selection per view id, set_selection, L1396, so two splits on one buffer keep independent cursors.

Syntax: tree-house Instead of Raw tree-sitter

Here the source diverges from most blog folklore about Helix: helix-core no longer depends on tree-sitter directly. Its Cargo.toml pulls in tree-house, the maintained wrapper crate the team factored the syntax engine into, helix-core/Cargo.toml, L35. Everything below that is still classic tree-sitter: grammars compiled to shared libraries, queries for highlights, injections, and locals.

The Syntax type wraps a tree_house::Syntax — a stack of language layers, one per injection (Markdown inside code fences, HTML inside Rust doc comments), with a hard PARSE_TIMEOUT of 500 milliseconds so a pathological file cannot stall the UI, Syntax, L514. The clever bit is Syntax::update: it converts the very same ChangeSet from the last edit into tree-sitter InputEdits and reparses incrementally, Syntax::update, L526. One data structure — the change set — serves undo, LSP sync, and syntax.

The Loader compiles each language’s highlight, injection, and locals queries once behind OnceLock caches and is shared across the app through an ArcSwap, so a theme or grammar refresh can swap it atomically, Loader, L275. For painting, a Highlighter walks the layer stack and emits HighlightEvent spans, Highlighter, L704 — the renderer consumes spans without ever holding a lock on the tree.

The Event Loop and the LSP Back Channel

helix-term/src/application.rs is where async Rust gets interesting. The Application owns the terminal, the compositor, the Editor, and the job pool, Application, L70. Its render method draws the compositor tree into a terminal buffer and positions a block cursor on the head side of the primary range, render, L261.

The loop itself is one tokio::select! marked biased over six streams, tokio::select!, L318: OS signals, terminal input, job callbacks, status messages, completed futures, and editor events. The biased flag matters: branches are polled in order, so input is never starved by a chattering background stream. A keypress lands in handle_terminal_events, which routes through the keymap and executes the matched command, handle_terminal_events, L700. Redraws are requested, not immediate — helix-event coalesces them so a burst of edits costs one frame.

Editor-internal traffic arrives as an EditorEvent: DocumentSaved, LanguageServerMessage, DebuggerEvent, IdleTimer, Redraw, or config updates, EditorEvent, L1351. Server messages specifically go through handle_language_server_message, which dispatches diagnostics, completions, and edit proposals, handle_language_server_message, L777.

The LSP side in helix-lsp is a study in async plumbing. Client is one server process with reader and writer tasks and a pending-request map, Client, L56. Client::call allocates a request id, registers a oneshot responder, and returns a future, call, L440, while notify fires fire-and-forget notifications, notify, L505. The Registry::get iterator resolves the right servers for a language and reuses clients whose workspace roots already match the document path, spawning only when needed, get, L705.

From Cargo Build to First Buffer

Building from source is straightforward if you have a recent toolchain — the workspace requires Rust 1.90 (Cargo.toml, L74). Clone the repo and run cargo build --release; the workspace’s default-members is just helix-term, so that single command produces the hx binary.

Three things trip people up. First, the runtime: hx searches for its runtime directory — queries, themes, grammars — at fixed locations, and HELIX_RUNTIME overrides the search path, runtime_dirs, L85. When you build from source you must make the repo’s runtime/ visible to the binary (the book documents the copy and hx --health shows what was actually found, book/src/install.md, L24). Second, grammars are not vendored binaries: run hx --grammar fetch to clone grammar sources listed in languages.toml and hx --grammar build to compile them, main.rs, L55. Skip that step and opening a Rust file silently falls back to regex highlighting. Third, pairing it with a fast terminal matters — the TUI redraws full frames, so something like Alacritty keeps latency honest. If you prefer tools that compose — ripgrep for search — Helix’s philosophy of small, sharp crates in one workspace will feel familiar.

Honest Limits

  • No plugin system. The book says extension points for diff providers will come from “a future plugin system”, book/src/editor.md, L431. Today, customization means keymaps, themes, language configs, and hook registration — not runtime plugins. If you need editor-level scripting, that is a real gap.
  • Syntax can silently downgrade. If a grammar’s shared library is missing, the loader logs “Skipping syntax config” and you get no tree-sitter features for that language, syntax.rs, L73. The failure is quiet by design.
  • The terminal backend is mid-migration. application.rs currently gates termina against crossterm per platform (application.rs, L64) — a transition visibly in flight in the tree, worth knowing before you build crates against unstable internals.
  • Highlighting has a budget. Parsing stops after the 500 ms PARSE_TIMEOUT noted above; enormous files may render stale spans rather than block, which is the right trade, but it is a cap, not magic.

None of these change the verdict: Helix is the clearest codebase we have toured for seeing how a modern editor actually works — every edit a composable transaction, every keystroke a command, every language feature a message over one merged stream.
entry.summary: How Helix implements Kakoune-style selection-first editing: ropey rope transactions, tree-house syntax, a tokio event loop, and async LSP clients inside a Rust workspace.

entry.title: Inside Neovim: How the RPC Core and Lua Host Actually Work

link.title: Inside Neovim: How the RPC Core and Lua Host Actually Work

entry.content:
Run nvim --headless +'lua print(vim.api.nvim_buf_line_count(0))' +qa on a file and you get an answer with no window, no terminal, no user. That is a strange property for an editor: the same binary you use interactively is also a scriptable service that speaks a binary protocol. It works because Neovim was restructured into something Vim never was — an event-loop core with an API surface, rather than a tangle of modal code with scripts bolted on.

The second oddity shows up in plugin behavior. Vimscript execution was famously blocking: call a job, wait, freeze the UI. In Neovim, plugins fire timers, watch jobs, and react to RPC notifications without the editor ever stalling. That is not magic either — it falls out of one design decision: everything, including your plugin callbacks, runs as events on a single libuv loop that the editor itself lives on.

So what actually happens between :lua vim.api.nvim_buf_set_lines(0, 0, 1, false, {"x"}) and a buffer changing on screen? This post walks the C source of src/nvim on master and traces that path end to end: bootstrap, the loop, the msgpack channel, the two scripting hosts, the buffer data model, and the redraw pass. Every symbol and line anchor below was verified against the tree.

Neovim from boot to redraw: the libuv loop, the msgpack-RPC channel, the two scripting hosts, the buffer data model, and the UI layer. Rendered from src/nvim on master.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Bootstrap is a strict sequence: main, L255 parses argv, runs early_init, L193 for the first option pass, then calls event_init, L158 at L284 to bring up the loop before any UI or user config exists.
  • There is exactly one loop object: the global Loop main_loop, L146, initialized by loop_init(&main_loop) at L160. Input, jobs, timers, signals, and RPC all multiplex through it.
  • Waiting is bounded: loop_poll_events, L78 delegates to loop_uv_run, L41, which invokes libuv uv_run at L59 in UV_RUN_ONCE mode — process one batch of I/O, then return so queued work executes promptly.
  • Events queue up through multiqueue_put_event, L134 into queues built by multiqueue_new, L86; child queues from multiqueue_new_child, L92, like the resize_events queue created at L162, flush along with their parent.
  • Remote clients attach because server_init, L35 binds --listen addresses; each accepted channel flips to RPC mode in rpc_start, L80, and decoded requests land in handle_request, L322.
  • One request can drive either scripting host: nvim_eval/nvim_exec2 from vimscript.c, L152, or nvim_exec_lua, whose real entry is nlua_exec, L1721 in the Lua host.
  • Buffer edits from any client go through nvim_buf_set_lines, L326, which splices lines, re-anchors extmarks via extmark_splice at L447, notifies watchers with changed_lines at L451, and repairs cursors with fix_cursor at L455.
  • Redraw is two-phase: redraw_all_later, L2715 only flags work, and the single pass update_screen, L483 turns flags into grid events that attached UIs consume.

The Event Loop That Runs Everything

Neovim’s core claim to modularity is that the editor and your plugins share one scheduler. event_init wires main_loop, and from then on every subsystem registers libuv handles on it: streams for channels, processes for :terminal and jobstart, timers for delayed work, signal watchers for SIGWINCH. When main() finishes bootstrapping, it settles into polling this loop and processing queues until teardown.

The mechanics matter. loop_poll_events, L78 takes a timeout in milliseconds, runs UV_RUN_ONCE, and then drains the queue that pairs with it. Because each poll handles at most one I/O batch before yielding to queued callbacks, no single subsystem can starve the others indefinitely — the editor interleaves RPC traffic, key handling, and redraw work in small slices. Events themselves are tiny structs: a function pointer plus an argument, appended with multiqueue_put_event, L134 and invoked when their queue is processed. Child queues matter for correctness: resize_events exists precisely so resize handling can be prioritized relative to the parent queue instead of being interleaved arbitrarily.

This loop is also why :terminal is honest about what it is — a real PTY child process streaming through the same loop, so an interactive shell such as fish runs in a split pane with the editor never blocking on it. If you know how event loops power language runtimes, the shape will feel familiar; it is the same idea Neovim imported, in C, with libuv.

msgpack-RPC: How Clients Talk to the Core

The API surface is reachable from inside (vim.api) and from outside over msgpack-RPC, and both paths converge on the same dispatch. Outbound-facing, server_init, L35 accepts --listen addresses (pipes and TCP sockets). When a client connects, rpc_start, L80 marks the channel as RPC and registers its read stream. Bytes are incrementally decoded by the msgpack unpacker (src/nvim/msgpack_rpc/unpacker.c), which emits either requests or notifications; requests carry a message id so the response, encoded by src/nvim/msgpack_rpc/packer.c, can be correlated.

handle_request, L322 resolves the method name to the generated handler for it — the same handlers vim.api calls in-process. That is the whole trick behind ecosystem tooling: an LSP client, a GUI, a test harness, or a plugin host built on Node all speak to identical API functions (nvim_eval at L152, nvim_exec2 at L54, and so on). Nothing about “remote” changes semantics.

One rule trips up new plugin authors: handlers that run as events on the loop may execute in a fast context where blocking calls are forbidden. Lua can detect this with nlua_in_fast_event, L1300, and the vim.call bridge nlua_call, L1317 actively rejects deferred-unsafe Vimscript functions with a hard error rather than deadlocking. This is why async plugins use vim.schedule/vim.defer_fn to hop back onto a safe queue slot — the guard rail lives right there in the bridge.

Hosting Lua and Vimscript Side by Side

Two interpreters share one process. The Vimscript evaluator is classic C: eval_expr, L594 parses an expression into a typval_T, descending through eval1, L1915 — a recursive-descent grammar whose atom level is eval7, L2650. Compound assignment operators like += route through eexe_mod_op, L201. Values stay in Vimscript’s own type system all the way down.

The Lua host is a different beast: a lua_State (global_lstate) embedded in the C process. Executing a chunk is three steps in nlua_exec, L1721: compile with luaL_loadbuffer at L1728, push the arguments as API Objects, and run under nlua_pcall, L330, which converts Lua errors into proper API errors instead of unwinding the editor. Values cross the boundary through conversion glue in src/nvim/lua/converter.c; buffers, windows, and tabpages surface in Lua as thin integer handles that call straight back into the API layer.

The bridges run both ways, which is what makes the dual-host model coherent. Vimscript reaches Lua via luaeval() and v:lua; Lua reaches Vimscript via vim.call/vim.fn through nlua_call. And the crossover is not just for callers: you can write a whole module in Lua and have Vimscript invoke it — nlua_call_typval, L1758 synthesizes a require('module').func(...) call with typval_T arguments, and Lua-implemented user commands execute through nlua_do_ucmd, L2405. The callable-bridging variant nlua_exec_typval_callable, L1691 handles calling a Lua function reference directly from Vimscript code. If you have ever embedded an interpreter in C — the way CPython embeds into C extensions — the pattern is the same; Neovim just applies it to a live editor instead of a REPL.

Buffers, Windows, and Change Propagation

The data model has three anchors. buf_T from buflist_new, L1984 is the text container; its contents live in memline structures, opened by open_buffer, L250 — whose comment is refreshingly literal: “open the memfile and read the file into memory.” Lazy loading exists too: buf_ensure_loaded, L222 opens the buffer only when needed, at L236. Windows (win_T) and tab pages are laid out by window.c, starting from win_alloc_first, L4345; a window never owns text, it views a buffer, which is why splits are cheap and why cursor repair after edits is per-window.

That repair step is visible right inside the API edit path. nvim_buf_set_lines performs a precise sequence: splice the requested line range, then extmark_splice, L447 re-anchors extmarks so decorations, LSP diagnostics, and plugin marks survive the edit with their semantics intact; changed_lines, L451 notifies every attached watcher — including remote RPC clients subscribed via nvim_buf_attach; and fix_cursor, L455 adjusts cursor positions in the affected windows. Editor events fire alongside: apply_autocmds, L1375 is the general entry for firing autocommand groups, and the grouped variant at L1481 does the matching work.

Redraw closes the loop. Editing code flags the screen via redraw_all_later, L2715 — it does not draw. The actual pass, update_screen, L483, runs later on the loop and turns accumulated flags into grid-level events. Because the UI layer (src/nvim/ui.c) abstracts the client protocol — ui_refresh, L189 reconciles which UI capabilities are active and pushes ui_call_option_set at L217 — the same core can serve the built-in TUI and external clients like a GUI or a GPU terminal such as alacritty. Scheduling respects the loop: ui_schedule_refresh, L288 puts a refresh event on resize_events with multiqueue_put at L290, so even redraw scheduling goes through the queue machinery rather than redrawing inline.

From Make Build to First Buffer

Building from source is deliberately boring. The repo uses CMake as its build system; BUILD.md documents the canonical steps: run make CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, and INSTALL.md shows installing with make install (optionally with CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX, or plain sudo make install). You do not hand-install the tricky dependencies — libuv, LuaJIT, tree-sitter and friends are fetched automatically into .deps/ by the deps build. Ninja is not required but is picked up automatically if present, which the docs recommend for faster builds. Building “PUC Lua” instead of LuaJIT is a supported variant via -DPREFER_LUA=ON, confirming LuaJIT is the default runtime, not a hard requirement.

Trace what happens when that freshly built binary starts: main() bootstraps options, event_init starts the loop, UI attaches, and the first buffer for your file materializes through open_buffer — memfile allocated, file read. From there the loop owns everything until +qa tears it down. That is the entire architecture in one breath: loop first, editor as events on the loop.

Honest Limits

The source is candid about its boundaries. The editor core — evaluator, buffer internals, redraw — is still C, and large C at that: eval.c is several thousand lines (eval_call_provider, L6602 sits near the end), drawscreen.c passes 2,700 lines, and main.c mixes CLI parsing with boot logic past the 2,000-line mark (do_user_initialization, L2131). Lua hosts the runtime layer (runtime/lua/vim/...) and calls into C through the API; it does not replace the C internals.

Vim9 script is not part of Neovim, and the tree says so directly: the lone Vim9 reference in src/nvim/runtime.c at L2728 is a comment noting Vim9 autoload is “not applicable to Nvim.” Neovim’s scripting story remains legacy Vimscript plus Lua, with Lua positioned as the forward path.

Also worth stating plainly: RPC requests execute on the main loop, single-threaded with the editor — the fast-context guards exist precisely because there is no worker thread to hide blocking calls in. And line anchors here are pinned to master on the date of this post; C files this active will drift.
entry.summary: How Neovim's libuv event loop, msgpack-RPC core, and embedded Lua host actually work, explained from src/nvim with pinned line anchors.

entry.title: Inside ripgrep: The Crate Architecture That Makes Search This Fast

link.title: Inside ripgrep: The Crate Architecture That Makes Search This Fast

entry.content:
You type rg 'fn walk_builder' in a checkout of ripgrep itself and the answer is on screen before your finger has left the Enter key. Run grep -r 'fn walk_builder' . on the same tree and you can hear the disk working: grep happily descends into target/, .git/, and every generated artifact your .gitignore exists to forget about. The speed gap is not one clever trick. It is a stack of small decisions — skip the right files, search the right way, use the right engine — wired together by an unusually disciplined crate architecture.

And ripgrep is honest about the second thing people notice: it respects .gitignore without being asked, skips hidden files and binary blobs, and still manages to be the fastest line-oriented searcher most of us have used. That combination sounds contradictory — filtering is work, and work costs time — until you read the source and see that every filter pays for itself by deleting future work.

This post walks that architecture in the actual tree (ripgrep 15.2.0, master). Between the moment you press Enter on rg pattern and the moment matches appear, roughly ten crates cooperate: a CLI front-end parses flags, a parallel walker streams candidate files while honoring gitignore rules, a layered regex engine stack matches text, and printers format the results. Two diagrams anchor the tour — an overview you can read left to right, and a detail graph for the internals. Every link below points at a real file and line in the upstream repository.

The full path of a single rg invocation: flags become a HiArgs config, the parallel walker yields gitignore-aware haystacks, the Searcher applies the regex engine to each one, and printers sink the matches. Left to right is the life of one search.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The driver is thin on purpose. run, L77 dispatches by mode: single-threaded search when -j 1, otherwise search_parallel — which never spawns threads itself; it just feeds a visitor closure to the walker at search_parallel, L175.
  • Flags become factories. walk_builder, L874 in HiArgs turns CLI options into a configured WalkBuilder, wiring -g globs, -t types, and the custom .rgignore filename.
  • The walker is the concurrency engine. WalkParallel::run, L1430 executes traversal on a worker pool whose size defaults to min(ncpu, 12) at threads, L1539 — parallelism sits exactly where the filesystem syscalls are.
  • Gitignore state is persistent. Ignore, L94 links each directory’s compiled matchers to its parent’s, so descending the tree never re-parses an ignore file.
  • Globs never match one by one. GlobSetMatchStrategy, L685 dispatches an entire set of patterns to specialized literal, extension, prefix/suffix or regex strategies in a single pass.
  • The engine probes with literals first. RegexMatcher, L367 bundles the full regex with an optional fast_line_regex — a cheaper matcher that never misses but may false-positive — used at find_candidate_line, L490.
  • Each file gets a strategy. search_path, L643 opens the haystack and tries a memory map first at mmap, L689, falling back to buffered streaming.
  • The hot loop is line-shaped. match_by_line_fast, L385 jumps straight to the next candidate match and sinks whole lines — no per-line allocation on the fast path.

The detail view: how flags become matchers, how the Ignore chain layers .gitignore/.ignore/.rgignore through GlobSet, how ConfiguredHIR compiles the engine, and where the 64 KB line buffer feeds the fast match loop.

A Workspace, Not a Monolith

The root Cargo.toml defines a single binary target — name = "rg" with path = "crates/core/main.rs" — plus nine workspace libraries: globset, grep, cli, matcher, pcre2, printer, regex, searcher, and ignore. crates/core is the only place that knows about a terminal; everything else is a plain library with a narrow job. matcher holds just the engine-agnostic Matcher trait, globset knows nothing about gitignore semantics, and the grep facade crate exists only to re-export the others under one name.

This shape has a practical payoff: the internals are reusable. Any tool can take the walker, the searcher and a matcher and assemble its own search command without inheriting a single CLI flag. It also keeps the crates individually benchmarkable — when a regression appears, the layer that caused it is visible in the structure, not buried in a 10,000-line main.rs. The workspace builds against Rust edition 2024 with a pinned rust-version of 1.96, which matters because the crates lean on recent regex-crate APIs. If you have read our Rust compiler source tour, this is the same workspace philosophy that the language’s own repo uses: many small crates, one thin binary shell.

The Regex Engine Stack: Literals Before Regex

When HiArgs::matcher() builds a matcher, the default path is grep-regex. Patterns are parsed into a ConfiguredHIR — an AST translated to a HIR that still remembers its configuration — and then compiled by to_regex with limits tuned for a CLI: a 10 MB one-pass DFA cap, a 1 MB full-DFA cap, and a 1,000-state limit. A pathological pattern fails to compile instead of hanging the search.

The interesting part is what wraps the compiled regex. RegexMatcher holds three fields: the real regex, an optional fast_line_regex, and a set of bytes that can never appear in a match. The fast regex is extracted from the pattern’s literals — for alternations like cat|dog|bird, it is just the alternation of those literals, which the underlying engine can match with memchr-class speed. During the line loop, find_candidate_line runs the probe first; only lines that survive go through the full regex. With -F/--fixed-strings, the builder skips regex parsing entirely and assembles the HIR from the literal bytes themselves. PCRE2 is optional behind the pcre2 feature: the PatternMatcher enum holds either a Rust regex or a PCRE2 matcher, -P selects it, and on 64-bit targets the builder enables the PCRE2 JIT with a 10 MB stack.

The Walker: Parallelism Where the Filesystem Is

ripgrep does not use a thread-pool crate. WalkParallel::run hands directories around a hand-rolled Message::Work/Quit loop — closer to the channel idioms you would write by hand in Go than to a generic scheduler. Each visitor callback runs on a worker thread that owns a clone of the SearchWorker, so searching is shared-nothing except for the output buffer.

Correctness lives in the Ignore chain. Every directory gets an IgnoreInner carrying matchers for custom ignore files, .ignore, .gitignore, and .git/info/exclude, plus a has_git flag. matched_ignore walks the parent chain and applies them in git’s precedence order, gated by require_git so gitignore rules only apply inside repositories. Each Gitignore wraps a GlobSet; matched strips the directory prefix and queries it with a reusable match pool. The semantics intentionally mirror git’s own implementation of these files — negations, directory-only patterns, anchoring — so a file git ignores is a file ripgrep skips, without shelling out to git.

Glob matching itself is where globset earns its keep. A GlobSet compiles its patterns once and dispatches on GlobSetMatchStrategy: exact literals go into a hash map guarded by a 64-bit length bitmap, basename literals match only the file name, and extension/prefix/suffix strategies cover the shapes gitignore files actually contain. Only genuinely regex-shaped globs fall back to a RegexSet, and even then a required-extension prefilter can reject a candidate before any pattern runs.

Memory Maps, Streaming and the 64 KB Line Buffer

For each haystack, Searcher::search_path opens the file and checks the mmap choice. The library default is never; the rg binary enables auto, and even then the heuristic only permits maps when searching at most ten explicit file paths, all of them regular files. macOS is excluded outright — a documented performance regression — and on Unix a successful map gets madvise(SEQUENTIAL). A memory map means zero copies: the kernel pages the file in and the regex engine scans the mapping directly.

Everything else streams. ReadByLine drives a fill/match loop over a LineBufferReader backed by a 64 KB LineBuffer, which also handles BOM sniffing and encoding transcoding. The rolling buffer lets ripgrep search files of any size with constant memory — including stdin and process output. Core::match_by_line picks the fast path only when the matcher itself is line-aware (is_line_by_line_fast checks that the matcher’s line terminator matches the searcher’s); that is exactly why single-line patterns get line_terminator(Some(b'\n')) at build time. Binary detection is folded into the same loop: a NUL byte in the buffer either stops the search or flags the file, so binary blobs cost one buffer fill, not a full scan.

From Cargo Build to First Search

Building is ordinary Cargo. Clone the repo, run cargo build --release, and you get one artifact: target/release/rg. There are no example binaries or daemons — the workspace’s other crates are libraries consumed by that single binary. The default build compiles without PCRE2; the optional engine is declared as features = { pcre2 = ["grep/pcre2"] }, so opting in means cargo build --release --features pcre2 on a machine with the PCRE2 C library available. The Debian packaging metadata enables that feature for release artifacts, and the release-lto profile ships with fat LTO, codegen-units = 1, and symbol stripping.

First search needs no setup: run rg TODO in any git checkout and the walker applies the repository’s .gitignore, skips hidden paths, and refuses to print binary garbage. Two flags change the plumbing rather than the results: -j controls walker threads, and --no-mmap forces the streaming path. --debug logs which layer made each decision, which is the fastest way to see the architecture in action.

Honest Limits

  • There is no index and no cache. Every invocation re-walks the tree. Speed comes from skipping work — ignored files, binary data, non-matching lines — not from remembering previous answers.
  • The default engine is Rust’s regex. Lookaround and backreferences require -P plus a build with the pcre2 feature and the native PCRE2 library installed.
  • Memory maps are best-effort. They are off on macOS, unused for directory walks or stdin, and a file truncated mid-search can abort the process — the reason the API is unsafe.
  • Sorting costs parallelism. Requesting --sort forces single-threaded traversal, so a sorted run is inherently slower on big trees.
  • Hidden and binary files stay hidden. The gitignore-aware defaults that make ripgrep pleasant can also surprise you; --hidden, --no-ignore, and -a exist precisely to undo them layer by layer.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of ripgrep's crate architecture: the parallel gitignore-aware walker, the regex engine stack with literal prefilters, globset, and the mmap-versus-streaming Searcher.
